passages.t: ‘Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt’
passages.happening:
The people hear the scouts' report and weep all night (verse 1). They turn on Moses and Aaron: “If only we had died in the land of Egypt, or if only we had died in this wilderness!” (verse 2). They ask why the LORD has brought them here to die by the sword. ‘Our wives and children will become plunder’ (verse 3). “So they said to one another, ‘Let us appoint a leader and return to Egypt’” (verse 4).

Moses and Aaron fall facedown. Joshua and Caleb tear their clothes and plead: “The land we passed through and explored is an exceedingly good land. If the LORD delights in us, He will bring us into this land” (verses 7-8). “Only do not rebel against the LORD, and do not be afraid of the people of the land” (verse 9).

“But the whole congregation threatened to stone Joshua and Caleb. Then the glory of the LORD appeared to all the Israelites at the Tent of Meeting” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This is the turning point of Numbers, and one of the great crises of the Old Testament. Everything in the book so far has been getting Israel ready for this moment. The people stand at the border of the land promised to Abraham, and they refuse to go in.

Their proposal is worse than panic. In the ancient world, to choose a new head was to renounce the old one, and to go back to Egypt was to renounce the exodus. They are not only turning down a plan of battle. They are undoing their own rescue.

Notice whom they blame. ‘Why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword?’ They have decided that God brought them out in order to kill them. The God who fed them every morning has become, in their minds, their enemy.

And notice their reason. They say they are afraid for their children. God will take up those very words.

The gestures in the passage were well known. Falling on one's face was the posture of a person begging before a superior or before God. Tearing one's clothes was the sign of grief or horror. Joshua and Caleb do it because they can see what is happening.

Their speech turns the frightened scouts' words around. The ten had said that the land devours its people. Joshua and Caleb say the people of the land ‘will be like bread for us’. Their protection is gone. The Hebrew word means their shade. And they give the one reason that matters: ‘the LORD is with us’. They do not argue that the walls are low. They argue that God is near.

The answer of the crowd is to reach for stones. Stoning was the community's punishment for the gravest crimes. Here it is aimed at the only two men telling the truth. At that moment God's glory appears, and the stoning stops before it begins.
passages.later:
Israel had said the same thing at the sea, a year before: “For it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness” (Exodus 14:12).

Nehemiah, confessing his people's history in prayer, remembered this night and what God did next: ‘They stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt. But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them’ (Nehemiah 9:17).

Stephen, a Jew speaking of his own ancestors, said that they ‘in their hearts turned back to Egypt’ (Acts 7:39).
passages.asks: Israel looked at the hard road ahead and decided that slavery had been better. Ask what you are tempted to go back to because the way forward frightens you. And ask whether you have ever, in fear, told yourself that God means you harm.

passages.happening:
God speaks to Moses. “How long will this people treat Me with contempt? How long will they refuse to believe in Me, despite all the signs I have performed among them?” (verse 11). He says he will destroy them and make of Moses a greater nation (verse 12).

Moses pleads. The Egyptians and the peoples of Canaan will hear of it, he says, and will conclude that the LORD was not able to bring his people into the land (verses 13-16). Then he quotes God's own words back to him: “The LORD is slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, forgiving iniquity and transgression” (verse 18). “Pardon, I pray, the iniquity of this people, in keeping with the greatness of Your loving devotion” (verse 19).

“‘I have pardoned them as you requested,’ the LORD replied” (verse 20).

Yet the men who saw God's signs and still treated him with contempt will not see the land (verses 22-23). Caleb will, because he ‘has a different spirit and has followed Me wholeheartedly’ (verse 24). Tomorrow the people are to turn back toward the wilderness (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
God's question in verse 11 names what has happened. The word is ‘believe’. It is the same Hebrew verb used of Abraham: “Abram believed the LORD” (Genesis 15:6). It means to rely on someone as firm. The people had seen the plagues in Egypt, the sea opened, the manna, the cloud. They had every reason to lean their weight on God, and they would not. The chapter does not call this weakness or ordinary fear. God calls it contempt.

God's offer to Moses is the same he made after the golden calf (Exodus 32:10): the people destroyed, and a new nation from Moses alone. For the second time Moses refuses to be great at his people's cost.

His prayer has two parts, and neither rests on Israel's merits. He does not say the people are sorry. He does not say they deserve another chance.

First he appeals to God's name among the nations. If Israel dies in the desert, Egypt will say that the LORD could start a rescue and could not finish it.

Then he appeals to God's own character. At Sinai, after the golden calf, God had told Moses who he is (Exodus 34:6-7). Moses now quotes that back, choosing the lines about patience and forgiveness. The key word is chesed, which the Berean Standard Bible renders ‘loving devotion’. It is love that keeps its promises even when the other side breaks theirs. Moses asks God to act like himself.

The word for ‘pardon’ in verses 19 and 20, salach, is used in the Hebrew Bible only with God as its subject. People are never said to do it. It is God's own kind of forgiving. And God does it. The nation will live. The promise will stand.

Then comes ‘Yet’. The hard question below takes up what the pardon did and did not mean.

Caleb is singled out for his ‘different spirit’. He had seen the same giants as the others.
passages.later:
Moses was quoting what God had said of himself at Sinai: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). No other description of God is quoted so often in the rest of the Old Testament.

The New Testament says of Jesus that “He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25). Moses standing between a guilty people and their judgment is a pattern of that. It is not a prediction made in this chapter.
passages.hard:
Did Moses change God's mind?

The chapter presents a real conversation. God announces destruction, Moses pleads, and God pardons. Christians have understood this in more than one way.

Many in the classical Christian tradition hold that God does not change his mind in the sense of being surprised or corrected. This same book says, “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind” (23:19). On this view the threat was a true statement of what the people deserved. It was spoken in a way that invited Moses to plead, and the prayer was itself part of God's purpose.

Others, including some recent theologians, read the passage as showing that God truly responds to prayer and alters his course because of it.

These notes take no side. Readers on both sides agree on what the passage is for. It means prayer for other people to be taken seriously. One man prayed, and a nation lived.
passages.asks: Moses did not plead the people's goodness. He pleaded God's name and God's character. Ask whom you could pray for today on those grounds alone, someone who has given you no reason to hope for them. And ask whether you believe that such a prayer matters.

passages.t: Forty years, a year for each day
passages.happening:
God speaks to Moses and Aaron. “How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me?” (verse 27). “As surely as I live, declares the LORD, I will do to you exactly as I heard you say” (verse 28).

The sentence follows. “Your bodies will fall in this wilderness—all who were numbered in the census, everyone twenty years of age or older—because you have grumbled against Me” (verse 29). Only Caleb and Joshua will enter the land (verse 30).

“But I will bring your children, whom you said would become plunder, into the land you have rejected—and they will enjoy it” (verse 31).

The children will be shepherds in the wilderness for forty years (verse 33). “In keeping with the forty days you spied out the land, you shall bear your guilt forty years—a year for each day” (verse 34).

The ten scouts who brought the bad report die of a plague. Of the twelve, ‘only Joshua son of Nun and Caleb son of Jephunneh remained alive’ (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The sentence is built from the people's own words. Each part of it turns something they said back on them.

They had said, ‘if only we had died in this wilderness’. They will. They had said their children would be carried off as plunder. The children are the ones who will inherit the land. The scouts had taken forty days to bring back a report of fear. The people will spend forty years, a year for each day. God says so himself: he will do ‘exactly as I heard you say’.

The forty years include the time already spent since Egypt. Deuteronomy counts thirty-eight years from Kadesh to the crossing of the Brook of Zered on the way to Moab (Deuteronomy 2:14).

The sentence falls on those counted in the census of chapter 1, the men of twenty and over. That is why the book has two counts. The first list is now a list of people who will die in the desert. The second, in chapter 26, will count their children.

The verb for grumbling in verses 27 and 29 is used almost only in the wilderness stories of Exodus and Numbers. It means resentful complaint that has gone on until it hardened into revolt. Honest lament, the kind the Psalms are full of, is a different thing. The Psalms bring their pain to God. This grumbling had decided against him.

Verse 33 is painful to read. The children ‘will suffer for your unfaithfulness’. They were not guilty, and they were not sentenced. They are promised the land. But they had to grow up in the desert while their parents' generation passed away. The chapter is honest that what one generation does falls on the next.

Joshua and Caleb had to walk the forty years too. The two men who trusted God shared the road with those who did not, and came out at the end of it.
passages.later:
Psalm 95 turns this day into a call to every later generation: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts as you did at Meribah, in the day at Massah in the wilderness” (Psalm 95:7-8).

The letter to the Hebrews builds its warning on that psalm. “And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?” (Hebrews 3:17). Then it turns to its readers: “Therefore, while the promise of entering His rest still stands, let us be careful that none of you be deemed to have fallen short of it” (Hebrews 4:1).

Paul and Jude use the story in the same way (1 Corinthians 10:5; Jude 1:5). In each case the warning is addressed to the church.
passages.hard:
If God pardoned the people in verse 20, why did they still die in the wilderness? And is this a threat hanging over anyone who doubts?

The pardon was real. God did not destroy the nation, and he did not take back his promise. Israel went on as his people. The manna kept falling for forty years. The cloud stayed. God's presence did not leave the camp.

But the pardon did not mean that the generation which refused the land would be given it anyway. They had said they did not want it, and God let that stand. Forgiveness kept Israel's future safe through its children. The refusal still shaped the lives of those who made it. Many readers have seen the same thing in ordinary life: a wrong can be truly forgiven, and some of its results remain.

The text does not say what became of these people before God when they died. It speaks of the land, and of a life spent in the wilderness. Moses himself, as chapter 20 will show, died outside the land, and no reader doubts where Moses stood with God. It would go beyond the chapter to say that everyone who died in the desert was lost for ever.

Two cautions belong here. First, this is not a story about the failings of the Jewish people. Israel's own Scriptures recorded it and sang it in worship as a warning to themselves (Psalm 95; Psalm 106), and the New Testament aims the same warning at Christians. Every use of the wilderness story in the New Testament is addressed to the church about its own heart.

Second, the people in this chapter were not troubled doubters. They had seen God's signs for more than a year, and they chose to appoint a leader and go back. A person who struggles to believe, who is afraid, who prays with a divided heart, is not the person this chapter describes.

If you are afraid that you have fallen away from God, that fear is not usually the mark of someone who has. Read Romans 8:38-39 slowly. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people were forgiven, and they still lived with what they had chosen. Ask what forgiven thing in your own life still has results you must live with, and whether you have mistaken those results for God's rejection. And ask what the children in your care are learning from the way you face what frightens you.

passages.t: Too late, and without the ark
passages.happening:
When Moses tells the people the sentence, they mourn bitterly (verse 39). Early the next morning they set out for the hills. “We have indeed sinned,” they say, ‘but we will go to the place the LORD has promised’ (verse 40).

Moses warns them. “Do not go up, lest you be struck down by your enemies, because the LORD is not among you” (verse 42).

“But they dared to go up to the ridge of the hill country, though neither Moses nor the ark of the covenant of the LORD moved from the camp” (verse 44). The Amalekites and Canaanites come down, attack them, and drive them back as far as Hormah (verse 45).
passages.hearers:
The chapter ends with one more reversal. The people who would not go up when God was with them now insist on going up when he is not.

It looks like repentance. They say, ‘We have indeed sinned.’ They are ready to do the very thing they refused the day before. But God had now told them to turn back toward the wilderness (verse 25). Yesterday's command had passed. To go up now was to disobey again, in the opposite direction.

The real fault was the same on both days. On the first day they would not trust God's promise. On the second they would not accept God's word of judgment. Both times they trusted their own reading of things.

Verse 44 gives the detail that explains the defeat. The ark did not move. Moses did not move. In chapter 10 the ark went ahead of the people to find them a resting place. Here they march without it. Courage was not what they had lacked. They had lacked God's presence, and they still did not have it.

Deuteronomy calls the enemy Amorites, a wider name for the peoples of the hills (Deuteronomy 1:44). The Amalekites were desert raiders of the south who had attacked Israel before, at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). Hormah lay in the southern desert of Canaan. Its exact place is debated.
passages.later:
Moses later described the rout: the enemy ‘chased you like a swarm of bees’ (Deuteronomy 1:44). And he added, “And you returned and wept before the LORD, but He would not listen to your voice or give ear to you” (Deuteronomy 1:45).

Paul draws a line between two kinds of sorrow that fits this scene: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
passages.asks: The people tried to mend their disobedience with an act of daring that God had not asked for. Ask where you have tried to make up for a failure by throwing yourself at something, when what was asked was to accept the consequence and walk the longer road. And ask what it would mean to move only when God's presence moves.
